items.title: Noah’s Ark Researcher Reveals DEATH Threats, Stunning New Radar Findings
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Whoa.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

The founder of an organization digging at a site in Turkey he believes could unveil the real-life Noah’s Ark has reportedly faced terrifying death threats and a burglary of his apartment.

Andrew Jones, founder of Noah’s Ark Scans, said it took years to get a permit from the Turkish government to be able to dig.

“For our efforts, it’s taken years, if not decades,” he said. “When you’re trying to get a permit, you have to work under a Turkish university, and it’s not just under the Turkish university; you’re working with a Turkish professor.”

Jones continued, “So here’s someone who’s going to say, ‘OK. I’m going to put my reputation on the line looking for Noah’s Ark, and then I’m going to go ahead and get go through the obstacles, and the time,’ and anything else being thrown at him or her to get a permit done.”

In addition to finding people willing to put their reputations on the line, Jones said you also need to have funding, which can be another barrier. Jones said he and his team had to act quickly once the permit was approved.

“It was the start of this year when we got the permit,” he said. “We had one month to basically fundraise, get organized, get people involved.”

Challenges still abound. The professor involved in the Noah’s Ark Scans project is reportedly being called a “traitor” to Turkey by some, with his atheist and agnostic friends also piling on.

Jones, too, has faced some challenges. He’s unsure whether the Noah’s Ark expedition sparked problems for him, but, months ago, he started having people pound on his door in the middle of the night earlier this year while issuing threats to kill him.

While motives are difficult to know, Jones said the chaos started after his team announced they received a permit.

“We made the mistake of announcing we had a permit,” he said. “In regards to like physical threats or robbery, I’ve never had that issue until this happened.”

The people pounding on the door in the middle of the night were “making threats and cursing in English.”

“They were targeting someone who they thought spoke English,” he said. “It wasn’t Turkish they were speaking. They were saying, ‘F you, and I’m going to kill you.'”

Jones called a friend to come over and examine the situation, but they never found the culprit. Then, just days later, it happened again. The Noah’s Ark Scans founder inevitably decided to leave the apartment altogether and stay with a friend out of abundance of caution.

His mission to find the Ark hasn’t stopped, and he has no plans to halt. Watch the video for the full story on where the expedition currently stands:

items.title: Alex Kendrick’s Blunt Message to Christians
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Encouraging.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Filmmaker Alex Kendrick is gearing up for a fascinating theatrical expedition as he and his brother, Stephen, prepare to return to their roots in a truly unique way.

In fact, the brothers are set to release, “Flywheel: Ignition of the Soul,” on Oct. 16, a remake of their popular 2003 movie, “Flywheel.”

“‘Flywheel’ was our very first movie shot in standard definition, not even high definition, over 20 years ago,” Alex Kendrick recently told CBN News. “And [I] kind of fell on my face thinking I could make a good feature film, and it turned out to be pretty low production quality.”

In fact, he said, he almost didn’t release the movie as he didn’t realize at the time how difficult filmmaking can be. Ultimately, though, the brothers proceeded — and the rest is history.

“The only thing I did right was beg God to use it,” Kendrick said. “And my brother Stephen helping me and saying, ‘We need to pray Ephesians 3:20 — that God would do exceedingly abundantly more than we could ask or imagine. So that’s the only thing we did right.”

Despite being green filmmakers at the time, the Kendricks were shocked to see how God showed up. “Flywheel” sold 1.3 million DVDs and had a massive response from audiences — much larger than they could have ever imagined.

“People said once they got over the production quality, like 10 minutes into it, then they were moved by the story, and they would come back and say, ‘I saw a version of myself on the screen,'” Kendrick said. “And the the Lord did what only the Lord can do by touching their hearts, and so we’ve always wanted to remake that, and higher quality over the years.”

That idea started coming to fruition two years ago, when the Kendricks were in Brazil releasing, “The Forge,” another faith-based film. The duo took some young Christian filmmakers through a boot camp and, through that experience and through prayer, the idea was birthed to work with teams there to remake, “Flywheel.”

“The Lord opened the door for us to remake, ‘Flywheel,'” he said. “We instantly got the funding, the support, the distribution, so we reshot it in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in Portuguese, and had wonderful cast and crew that love the Lord help us make it, and so it’s made in their culture, their language. They’re so thrilled about it.”

Kendrick said pre-screenings of the film have left audiences crying and cheering. The movie has now been dubbed for Americans audiences into English. Regardless of the language in which the film is viewed, Kendrick believes audiences will love it.

“This movie that talks about lordship and is now modernized [and] is coming out in theaters Oct. 16,” he said. “Can’t wait to see what the Lord does with this one.”

Kendrick believes this movie is releasing at the right cultural moment, with the main character working as a successful used car salesman when he goes through a very dark time in his life. This man realizes he needs more than his own logic to navigate it all, seeking help in marriage, fatherhood — and more. It’s his newfound faith in Jesus that changes everything.

“We do not need more lukewarm Christians,” Kendrick said. “What we need is Christians who are sold out and truly followers of Jesus Christ.”

He continued, “When people see the life of a Christian, what they don’t need to see is half-hearted commitment to our Savior, and half-hearted integrity. They need to see someone who lives for a higher purpose, because we serve an almighty God and that the way we live bears fruit of that relationship.”

Kendrick is hoping — much like the first “Flywheel” — people see themselves on the screen and confront spiritual issues in their own lives.

items.title: Sam Altman Is ‘Very Uncomfortable’ With People Treating AI Like a Religion
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: On Oct. 1, an X user asked Grok, Elon Musk’s chatbot, to remove the “fake gods” from an image of Jesus standing among other deities. Grok sent back Jesus alone and replied “Done.” Then it kept going. It said Jesus “did not qualify” as a fake god and called him “a historical figure with strong…
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

On Oct. 1, an X user asked Grok, Elon Musk’s chatbot, to remove the “fake gods” from an image of Jesus standing among other deities. Grok sent back Jesus alone and replied “Done.”

Then it kept going. It said Jesus “did not qualify” as a fake god and called him “a historical figure with strong contemporary attestation.” And: “I affirm that Jesus is the Son of God and that God raised him from the dead.”

The post went viral. It was later deleted.

Two days later, Sam Altman posted on X that he is “very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models.” He called it “a real safety issue.” The OpenAI CEO, who has 6.3 million followers on X, didn’t name anyone, and he didn’t say what set him off. The post doesn’t mention Grok, Anthropic or the pope.

I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue.

— Sam Altman (@sama) October 3, 2026

It was a busy week for AI and religion. On Sept. 29, The New York Times reported that Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah has met with religious leaders, including Vatican officials, about whether the company’s Claude models might be conscious or have moral status. Anthropic’s internal document on Claude’s values is known as the “Soul Doc.”

The report said Olah had floated models going to something like Catholic confession to admit mistakes and shape future behavior, and that before a Vatican event in May he urged advisers to the pope to take machine consciousness “more seriously.”

On Oct. 2, Pope Leo XIV told the church to team up with artists to protect human creativity. He said it’s “urgent to distinguish human art from what machines produce” and that there’s “an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate.” His most-quoted line: “Algorithms lack the spark of humanity.” Altman posted the next day.

Dario Amodei, who runs Anthropic, used to work with Altman at OpenAI. And Altman has wandered into this territory before. In a 2023 interview with the Financial Times, he described OpenAI’s products as channels into “magic intelligence in the sky.”

He’s not the only one in the industry pushing back. Jon Barron, a principal research scientist at Google DeepMind, posted on X that he’s “disturbed” by researchers trying to elevate the moral standing of AI systems and urged others to “reject this movement.”

Altman has said he’s “somewhat confused” about whether God exists.

items.title: Analyzing the Theological Arguments for Abortion Abolitionism
items.author: Dr. Kody W. Cooper
items.summary:
Dr. Kody W. Cooper

The abortion abolitionists’ foundational claim to bear the exclusive mantle of Christianity is as arrogant as it is absurd.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Kody W. Cooper

For several years now, the so-called abolitionist movement in abortion politics was considered the fringe of a fringe. But the movement is gaining traction, and a recent debate sponsored by Students for Life of America’s Demetree Institute for Pro-Life Advancement spotlights key strategic cleavages dividing pro-lifers. But do the abolitionists’ theological and biblical arguments withstand scrutiny? First, a bit of context.

Beginning about a decade ago, abolitionists in Texas called for ignoring Roe v. Wade and Planned Parenthood v. Casey in defiance of the Supreme Court and abolishing abortion at the city, county, and state levels. They channeled the spirit of an argument some leading pro-life constitutional scholars have long held as a plausible interpretation of the Fourteenth Amendment: that all persons, born and unborn, are deserving of equal protection of the laws. Yet if this constitutional argument were adopted, it would entail a “maximalist” pro-life outcome of outlawing abortion across a nation in which many states have strong majorities that support it. And it has found scarce support among originalist judges. Whether for principled or prudential reasons, or both, they favored the view that the Constitution is silent on abortion and thus left the issue to the people of the various states to decide. In the Roe–Casey years, mainstream pro-lifers sought to marshal support for incremental pro-life laws that would survive constitutional challenges and save as many babies as possible. In the four years since Dobbs returned authority to legislate on abortion to the states, pro-lifers have continued to work incrementally as the abolitionist movement has called for abolition now by extending equal protection of state laws against murder to unborn children—and holding all parties to abortion criminally liable, including mothers. As evident in the White Rose Resistance statement, for example, several prominent conservative Christian influencers have signed onto a version of abolitionism.

While many abolitionists offer these arguments in good faith, many mainstream pro-lifers are not convinced. (For the sake of simplicity, I’ll refer to mainstream pro-lifers who prefer incrementalist strategies simply as “pro-lifers,” a terminological distinction the abolitionists themselves adopt). Pro‑lifers argue that criminal immunity for mothers was and continues to be prudent. In the first place, while abortion was historically a crime at common law in the United States, there is no tradition of widespread prosecution for the crime. Indeed, it has hardly ever been prosecuted in American history (perhaps only three attempts). This was partly because it is a hard crime to detect and prove. This difficulty is arguably more acute now, when most abortions are chemical abortions induced by mifepristone, which is not detectable by blood tests and presents like a miscarriage. In a post-Dobbs world, pro-lifers also argue we need to account for the noetic effects of a half-century of lies perpetuated by the institutions of law, courts, media, and education, which have deceived many women into believing the unborn aren’t persons. If correct, many women seeking abortion may lack the requisite mens rea (“guilty mind”) to prosecute them for murder. Moreover, pro-lifers maintain that it was and remains more feasible and politically palatable to focus on prosecuting abortionists than mothers, particularly in light of the consistent majority of public opinion over the last thirty years favoring legal abortion in all or some cases. And pro-lifers contend that the implication of implementing abolitionist measures in this moment—and potentially subjecting mothers to the death penalty in states like Texas—will generate a massive backlash against pro-life legislators and the movement more generally.

In the recent debate, mainstream pro-lifer JoJo Ruba ably defended his view. Meanwhile, the Foundation to Abolish Abortion president Bradley Pierce’s theological and biblical arguments warrant a detailed analysis. The interlocutors stipulated that they agreed on the ultimate goal of full equal protection of the laws for the unborn—their debate was over the means. According to Pierce, pro-life incrementalism is contrary to “God’s way” and the “Christian way.” 

Abolitionism is “God’s way” because the Bible tells us so. The Bible defines human life as beginning at conception, proscribes murder, and mandates murder be punished as a matter of both retribution and deterrence. Moreover, laws that exempt mothers from criminal liability for abortion violate the Bible’s proscription of “partiality,” a claim for which various Bible verses are cited. And how should this program be communicated to a largely post-Christian society? Pierce explicitly pooh-poohs appeals to instruments of persuasion like science, history, and natural reason, insisting instead on a form of divine command voluntarism and biblicism: “It is about Christ is King, and he says don’t murder people.” The suggestion is that when pro-lifers do not end every argument or pro-life law with, because Christ is King, they are dishonoring God. God’s way is to argue and legislate with proof‑texts from the Bible. And if the audience does not accept the authority of the Bible? Then, more cowbell: Preach unto them the Bible!

“God’s way” thus looks strikingly like a Reformed Protestant evangelical postmillennialism. While a kind of postmillennialism—the idea that Christ’s thousand-year reign will come after Christian evangelism of the world has largely been achieved—is not per se contrary to Catholic teaching, biblicism is. It is also out of step with the best of the American political tradition. I can’t help but recall Alexander Hamilton’s exhortation to Samuel Seabury, which Pierce would do well to heed: “Apply yourself, without delay, to the study of the law of nature.” That is, Pierce simply overlooks what the Bible calls the law “written on the heart” and how natural law theory was cultivated and preserved even by the best theologians in his own Reformed tradition, such as Francis Turretin.

If Pierce had attended to the study of Reformed masters like Turretin, he would have learned that the evidence of the existence of a moral law known in conscience by unaided reason is affirmed in Scripture, apparent by the common consent of nations, apparent to the individual conscience, an implication of God’s governance over rational creatures who have not received or heard or accepted revelation, and testified to by the noble pagan philosophers (Institutes of Elenctic Theology). Accordingly, when St. Paul preached on Mars Hill to the men of Athens, he didn’t beat them over the head with the Pentateuch, an authority they did not recognize, but instead appealed to their natural knowledge of God manifest in creation. Hence, morally reasoning with pagans in a way that appeals to the law written on the heart, without explicitly invoking Christ’s kingship as the pedigree of that law, is no dishonor to God. Similarly, a law that focuses on aiding women in crisis pregnancy or saving babies, which is not prefaced with an invocation of the Holy Trinity, is not an act of vice for that reason. It is rather an act of virtue that is referable to God’s glory.
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

If indeed the natural law is—as natural lawyers from Aquinas to Turretin taught—the eternal law of God impressed upon his creatures and made known to reason, what difference does that make for the debate between abolitionists and pro-lifers? Well, the natural law is expressed in positive law in two ways. First, by way of deduction. So a deduction from the moral principle do not steal is to make theft a crime in human positive law. But how shall thieves be punished? This is the realm of determinatio, in which legislators reason from general principles to specific conclusions by exercising the virtue of prudence to determine just what sorts of punishments would conduce to the common good, to justice and peace. Simply put: It is entirely possible that abolitionists and pro-lifers could have a good-faith disagreement over what sorts of punishments for the crime of abortion would be prudent (would be enforceable, save more babies, assist women in crisis pregnancies, encourage women to visit pregnancy resource centers, change women’s hearts, convert the culture of death to a culture of life, and the like). Mr. Ruba’s arguments on these and other prudential points deserve serious consideration.

It is fatuous to dismiss these considerations by crying partiality, as if prudence had no bearing on whether a legal classification that benefits or burdens a particular class of persons has any rational basis. That is not what the Bible teaches. The biblical injunction is clearly intended to require a judicial virtue forbidding favoritism of a disputant for arbitrary reasons or reasons unrelated to justice, like his poverty or wealth. Meanwhile, under the Old Law, all sorts of discriminations with a rational basis were permitted. For example, only descendants of Aaron of the Levites could serve as priests (Num 3:10), usury could be charged to foreigners but not fellow Jews (Deut 23:20), and debts owed to fellow Israelites were cancelled every seven years but not debts owed to foreigners (Deut 15:3). 

None of this is to suggest a Catholic natural lawyer could not arrive in good conscience at a version of equal protection, particularly when cultural realities are favorable. Indeed, there are various Roman Catholic countries that impose criminal sanctions on mothers for abortion (even if prosecution of them is rare) that appear to be in accord with natural law principles (as in Malta). 

But I am suggesting that the abolitionists’ foundational claim to bear the exclusive mantle of Christianity is as arrogant as it is absurd. The idea that one peculiar Reformed biblicist outlook just is “God’s way”—and the implication that the pro-life incrementalism is the way of the infidel—distorts the Bible, is ignorant of the broad Christian natural law tradition, and is an insult to the millions of pro-lifers who have honored God for decades with their tireless work to love mothers and save babies.

items.title: Tuesday, October 13, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus declares the value of almsgiving: “As to what is within, give alms, and behold, everything will be clean for you.”
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Galatians 5:1-6

For freedom Christ has set us free. Stand firm, therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.

Listen! I, Paul, am telling you that if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you. Once again I testify to every man who lets himself be circumcised that he is obliged to obey the entire law. You who want to be justified by the law have cut yourselves off from Christ; you have fallen away from grace. For through the Spirit, by faith, we eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything; the only thing that counts is faith working through love.

Psalm
Psalm 119:41, 43, 44, 45, 47, 48

Let your steadfast love come to me, O Lord,
    your salvation according to your promise.
Do not take the word of truth utterly out of my mouth,
    for my hope is in your ordinances.
I will keep your law continually,
    forever and ever.
I shall walk at liberty,
    for I have sought your precepts.
I find my delight in your commandments,
    because I love them.
I revere your commandments, which I love,
    and I will meditate on your statutes.

Gospel Reading
Luke 11:37-41

While he was speaking, a Pharisee invited him to dine with him; so he went in and took his place at the table. The Pharisee was amazed to see that he did not first wash before dinner. Then the Lord said to him, “Now you Pharisees clean the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. You fools! Did not the one who made the outside make the inside also? So give for alms those things that are within; and see, everything will be clean for you.

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus declares the value of almsgiving: “As to what is within, give alms, and behold, everything will be clean for you.”

Almsgiving is valuable because we’re members of a mystical body—we’re implicated in each other. I can never say that your suffering is not mine or that your neediness is not mine. All of us are co-implicated. We’re responsible for each other, and giving alms is a very concrete way to acknowledge that. When we share gifts or charity with those in need, we’re acknowledging the fact that we’re not in this alone, that the things that we own are meant for others. Almsgiving is also tied to the corporal and spiritual works of mercy, which every Catholic is obligated to practice every day.

Numerous spiritual masters have witnessed that belief in God is strengthened not so much from intellectual effort as from moral action. When a man asked the English Jesuit poet Gerard Manley Hopkins what he must do in order to believe, Hopkins replied, “Give alms.” As you love through tangible acts, you will come to believe more deeply and to enter more fully into friendship with God.
